extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of literature; readers of Montaigne and those interested in reading/criticism/historiography
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical criteria for reading, judging, and writing literature and history as expressed in a personal essay. Covers reading habits, qualities of good poetry, drama, historiography, eloquence, and the nature of virtue as a standard of moral evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness of understanding and judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for critics and authors who can 'unplume' the reader by clearness of understanding and judgment and by distinguishing the force and beauty of the discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise is due to those who expose errors clearly; value rests in the ability to show the measure of one's sight by clear, forceful, and beautiful discourse. Anti-pattern: praise or reputation that masks lack of clear judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confession of ignorance as testimony of judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Confessing one's ignorance is one of the surest testimonies of sound judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admit limits of understanding; many faults escape our eye, and true judgment includes acknowledging what we cannot discern when pointed out by others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural, unforced writing pace
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should show their natural and ordinary pace; write as things come to them, irregular as it is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer writing that jogs on at its own rate rather than laboured, artificially regular prose. Anti-pattern: forced regularity and overworking material to appear polished at the cost of naturalness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read for pleasure first; do not overburden oneself for perfect knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Read to please oneself by honest diversion; only study for self-knowledge—how to die and live well—and do not 'buy' perfect knowledge at excessive cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid turning reading into an onerous task; favour ease over labour. Anti-pattern: insisting on mastering every difficulty at the cost of losing time and pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impatient reading: abandon books that do not immediately please
rubrics_metrics.description: An impatient understanding must be satisfied at first; what is not discerned at once becomes more obscure by continued insistence, so give up a book after a charge or two if it does not please.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do nothing without gaiety; prolonged, obstinate endeavour darkens and tires judgment. Practical rule: if one book does not please, take another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer looseness and short pieces for casual study
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor authors whose works consist of loose pieces that do not require prolonged reading—allowing the reader to take them up and lay them down at pleasure (e.g., Plutarch's minor works, Seneca's epistles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These works suit readers who cannot sustain long, continuous study; they provide useful, true opinions delivered plainly. Anti-pattern: long, heavily sequenced treatises that demand sustained attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer older works and those intelligible in one's language
rubrics_metrics.description: Old books often seem fuller and stronger; avoid authors in languages one cannot perfectly understand (e.g., Greek works) because imperfect intelligence of the material weakens judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose works you can fully grasp; do not force admiration for works whose language you do not adequately know.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of good poetry: elegance, polish, perpetual sweetness
rubrics_metrics.description: The best poets (e.g., Virgil, Lucretius, Catullus, Horace) exhibit elegance, equal polish, perpetual sweetness, and flourishing beauty rather than affected 'stings' or forced flamboyance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admire sustained grace and polish (Catullus's epigrams) over bitter epigrams or excessive ornament. Example: Virgil's Georgics and the fifth book of the Aeneid as models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affectation and fantastical elevations in poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Good judgment admires ancients who avoided affectation, fantastical Spanish/Petrarchic elevations, and overstated touches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should not hunt after unnatural elevations or softer ornamental touches; anti-patterns include contrived Petrarchan mannerisms and affectation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegance of diction should not be a mere substitute for substance
rubrics_metrics.description: While elegance can occupy the reader and cause one to forget the plot, it should not be used simply to mask lack of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good writers rely on both substance and style; poor playwrights load their works with borrowed matter because they lack strength in language. Anti-pattern: relying on story to cover weak language or vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good comedy/drama should not over-burden plots or borrow excessively
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern comedic writers often take multiple plots from Plautus or Terence or cram several novels into one play to compensate for a lack of original material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overloading matter; strong comedies sustain themselves on language and character rather than spliced-together plots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural performance and modest presentation over grotesque affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Good actors/drolls in their everyday appearance, with natural faces and manner, give full pleasure; apprentices resort to painted faces, disguises, and grotesque tricks when they lack innate art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer natural representation and simplicity over exaggeration and mechanical trickery in performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of good historians: eyewitness or participant, fidelity, and full reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: The only good histories are written by those who held command in the affairs they write of, participated in them, or at least commanded others; such accounts tend to be accurate and avoid large errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer histories from direct actors (Greek and Roman models). Bad historians: those who write from hearsay, chosen for eloquence rather than knowledge. Anti-patterns: historians who twist judgment for advantage, omit well-known facts, or shape narrative to bias (e.g., apologia rather than history).

rubrics_metrics.name: Value simplicity and frank correction in historical writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple historiographers (e.g., Froissart) who record faithfully, confess and correct errors, and represent varied rumours provide raw matter from which readers may form judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such plain, honest narratives leave readers something to judge and are valuable despite imperfections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the 'middle sort' historian who chews the reader's meat
rubrics_metrics.description: Middle sort historians select and judge events, often inclining history to their own fancy, omitting inconvenient particulars, and altering substance by abridgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warn against historians who 'judge for us' rather than present material to be judged; authors should avoid over-selection and leave material in its substance for readers to assess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous inquiry and confrontation of witnesses for historical truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The inquisition after truth is delicate; one cannot accept a battle report from the commander or soldiers without confronting witnesses and considering objections to every incident's proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical truth may require judicial-like cross-examination of witnesses; do not trust singular accounts without corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preface and rhetorical ornaments can be wasteful; begin with the main proposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Cicero's prefaces, definitions, divisions, and etymologies often smother the life of his work; Montaigne prefers authors who begin with the main proposition rather than prolonged preparation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a reader who wants to become wise rather than learned, logical and aristotelian dispositions are of little use; avoid authors who aim to 'render me attentive' by ritualistic preliminaries. Anti-pattern: prolonged 'Hoc age' preliminaries that tire rather than whet appetite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer shorter, rounder style in eloquence
rubrics_metrics.description: A shorter style comes more roundly off; long cadences and repeated phrases (e.g., 'esse videatur') are criticized in oratory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conciseness and brisker shuffling of parts are preferable to long-winded periods; value brevity and directness in speech and writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotate reading with end-time and judgment to aid memory
rubrics_metrics.description: As an aid to weak memory, note at the end of every book the time when finished and the judgment made of it to represent the character and general idea conceived of the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical habit: write brief annotations summarizing one's judgment to help recall and future navigation of one's library.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between goodness and virtue: difficulty as test of virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Goodness (being naturally well-disposed) differs from virtue; virtue presupposes difficulty and contention and is strengthened by encountering pain, necessity, and contempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True virtue seeks occasions to be tested and fortified by combat (example: Epaminondas, Metellus, Socrates). Anti-pattern: equating mere good nature or passive goodness with full virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mischaracterize philosophical schools; Epicurean steadiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not accept vulgar opinions that Epicureans are lax compared to Stoics; some Epicureans display rigour and a love of honour and justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid polemical or unjust attributions; assess philosophical schools by their exemplars and actions rather than popular caricature.
